text: Kafka's broker default is log.retention.hours = 168 (7 days) with cleanup policy 'delete'. Per topic you can set retention.ms = -1 to keep data indefinitely, or use log compaction to keep the latest value per key.
why: Corrects the 'kept forever by default' idea with the actual defaults and how to change them.

text: In Kafka, auto.offset.reset decides where a consumer group with no committed offset starts; the default is 'latest', so a brand-new group skips existing messages unless set to 'earliest'.
why: A new consumer starting from the horizon is a setting, not the default.

text: Adding partitions to a Kafka topic is an online operation, but it changes the key-to-partition mapping: records with the same key may go to a different partition afterwards, and existing data is not moved.
why: Repartitioning by hashtag relies on stable key routing, which a partition change briefly breaks.

text: Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so the partition count caps how many consumers in a group can work in parallel; extra consumers stay idle.
why: Clarifies that partitions bound, rather than dictate, the worker count.

text: If a counting server commits its Kafka offsets only after writing count += n to the database, a crash between the two re-processes that batch, giving at-least-once delivery and an over-count. That is exactly the recount L-0255 accepts.
why: Ties the 'may recount' compromise to the offset-commit order that causes it.

text: DynamoDB's atomic counters (UpdateItem with SET c = c + :n) are not idempotent: a retried update after a timeout can over-count. AWS suggests conditional updates where over- or under-counting can't be tolerated.
why: Atomic increments are safe under concurrency but not under retries.

text: Kafka Streams performs this repartitioning automatically: grouping by a new key (groupBy) writes the records to an internal repartition topic keyed by the new key before aggregating.
why: Shows the hashtag-extractor step is a standard, built-in stream-processing operation.

text: Redis Streams, unlike Redis Pub/Sub, persist messages and support at-least-once delivery with consumer groups, so they are the Redis option when messages must survive subscriber downtime.
why: Gives the Redis alternative that would have avoided the data-loss objection.

text: The Kafka producer already buffers unsent records in memory (buffer.memory, default 32 MiB) and retries until delivery.timeout.ms (default 120 s) before reporting failure. The 'buffer in memory' option is partly built in.
why: Learners should know the client's default behaviour before adding their own buffer.

text: In SQS, a dead-letter queue receives messages that consumers failed to process after maxReceiveCount attempts. Kafka Connect has its own DLQ setting (errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name) for records a connector could not process.
why: Clarifies what 'dead letter queue' means in the products named.

text: In the transactional outbox pattern, the service inserts the outgoing message into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business update. A separate relay process then publishes it to the broker.
why: Gives the precise definition of the pattern named in class.

text: Kafka tiered storage (production-ready since Kafka 3.9) moves completed log segments to remote storage such as S3 or HDFS while keeping them readable through Kafka; a RemoteStorageManager plugin must be supplied.
why: Names the current built-in feature behind 'plugins that archive to S3'.

text: Managed-Kafka SLAs vary: Amazon MSK credits customers when Multi-AZ availability falls below 99.9% in a month, while Confluent Cloud offers 99.99% for multi-zone clusters (99.5% for Basic).
why: Replaces a single 'Kafka = 99.9%' figure with real, deployment-dependent numbers.

text: MongoDB's data-modelling guide says duplicating data avoids joins on reads, but 'if the duplicated data is updated often, using a reference ... may be a better approach'.
why: Vendor guidance for the post-ID vs embedded-post trade-off.

text: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) means using a different model to update information than the model used to read it. Martin Fowler credits Greg Young, and notes it fits event-based systems and is often split into services that communicate with events.
why: Gives the correct definition so CQRS isn't equated with Kafka.

text: Kinesis lets a reader start at TRIM_HORIZON (oldest retained record), LATEST, AT_TIMESTAMP, or at or after a specific sequence number.
why: Names the exact start positions behind 'horizon / checkpoint / current'.

text: In current Python docs, cProfile is an alias of profiling.tracing (deterministic). The docs recommend the sampling profiler for production debugging and tracing for development and testing.
why: Points Python users to the production-safe option.

text: Continuous (sampling) profilers are built to run everywhere: Datadog says its Continuous Profiler 'runs in production across all services' with minimal CPU and memory impact.
why: Profiling need not be limited to canaries with modern tools.

text: DRM restricts playback, but it cannot attribute a leak once the screen is recorded. Leakers are identified with forensic watermarking, which embeds an invisible viewer-specific mark in each copy.
why: Names the technology that actually identifies leakers.

text: In Knit Pro International v. State of NCT of Delhi (20 May 2022), India's Supreme Court held that Section 63 copyright infringement (6 months to 3 years plus fine) is cognizable and non-bailable.
why: Gives the actual legal basis for the teacher's claim.

text: AWS says RDS Multi-AZ DB instance failovers 'are typically 60-120 seconds', and clients must reconnect because the DNS record changes.
why: Gives a realistic failover figure for planning timeouts and retries.

text: Cassandra describes its leaderless design as multi-master replication: every replica can accept writes, and conflicting updates are resolved by last-write-wins timestamps (so clocks need NTP).
why: Shows the concrete conflict-resolution cost the teacher alluded to.

text: Go's GOMAXPROCS (default: number of CPU cores) limits how many goroutines execute at once; goroutines themselves start with a few-kilobyte stack, so hundreds of thousands can exist in one process.
why: Separates 'more goroutines' (memory) from 'more parallelism' (CPU).

text: Kafka's co-creator Jay Kreps argues 'it's okay to store data in Kafka': with unlimited retention or compaction it can be a system of record, which 'does mean raising the bar for how you run it'.
why: Balances the 'never a source of truth' rule with the counter-view from Kafka's authors.
